scope: Diff-based PR-gate security review of git range 0fa9bec732530310f6e0fccdcd495ab23d22432b..dc66121c640a348bc18597e520363d849a360bd7 (integration-branch tip .. feature-branch head), gating the rc-2 feature -> integration PR of the ship cycle publishing as 0.4.5. The range is exactly two commits: the consumption (deletion) of the rc-1 security verdict handoff after its PR merged, and the version mint plus changelog fold. Totals: 3 files, +13/-76 (net -63 LOC) -- the changelog, the packaging manifest, and the deleted verdict handoff. Zero production files and zero test files are touched, and no CI/workflow or IaC file is touched (the repo carries no container, compose or infrastructure-as-code definition at all). Method: confirm the changed-path set exactly matches the declaration; verify the version mint against the live package index rather than the commit message, since a lower-numbered mint is the shape that causes downgrade-shadowing; confirm version single-sourcing; scan every added line for secrets, PII and private names; confirm the deleted verdict is the correct consumed artifact and that no verdict survivor remains; review the publication credential path that this cycle will exercise; and spot-check the specs doctor for a version-pin interaction. The full test suite was NOT re-run, per instruction -- preflight is reported green at the range head. No exploit code, penetration tool or network scanner was run; the only network call was a read-only query of the public package index metadata.
verdict_reason:
APPROVED at dc66121c for the rc-2 gate. None of the mandatory REQUEST_CHANGES triggers fires: no secret or credential appears in the range, no test is disabled, no dependency moves, no untrusted input reaches a privileged sink, and public-asset privacy is unaffected because no public asset is touched.

SCOPE CONFIRMED EXACTLY AS DECLARED. `git diff --name-status` over the range returns exactly three paths and nothing else: `M CHANGELOG.md`, `M pyproject.toml`, and `D` the consumed rc-1 verdict handoff. Totals +13/-76 (net -63 LOC). Decisively, filtering the same range to the production package AND the test tree returns EMPTY -- not one line of code or test changed, so no executable attack surface moved and every module-level conclusion of my rc-1 review carries forward untouched.

THE VERSION MINT IS THE ONLY THING IN THIS RANGE THAT CAN HURT ANYONE, AND I VERIFIED IT AGAINST THE LIVE INDEX RATHER THAN TRUSTING THE COMMIT MESSAGE. `pyproject.toml` changes exactly one line pair, the version, from the internal spec-release id to `0.4.5`. Minting a LOWER-looking number than the repo previously carried is exactly the shape that produces a supply-chain accident: if any `0.5.x` had ever been published, then publishing `0.4.5` afterwards would leave the newer code sitting behind a lower version while resolvers kept serving the older, higher-numbered artifact -- a silent downgrade-shadowing of the entire release. So I queried the package index directly and enumerated every published version. Findings: the published set is `0.1.0, 0.1.1, 0.1.2, 0.1.4, 0.1.5, 0.1.6, 0.2.0, 0.2.1, 0.2.2, 0.2.3, 0.3.0, 0.4.0, 0.4.1, 0.4.2, 0.4.4`; the index's own `info.version` is `0.4.4`; NO `0.5.x` has ever been published (empty set); and `0.4.5` is not taken. Therefore `0.4.5` is a strict, contiguous increment over the true latest, it collides with nothing, it shadows nothing, and a resolver will correctly serve it as the new highest version. The CHANGELOG's honesty amendment -- that the earlier internal id was staged but its publication was retained and never approved at the release gate -- is CONFIRMED TRUE by the index, not merely asserted. Correcting that sentence removes a false provenance claim from shipped documentation, which is an integrity improvement in its own right.

VERSION SINGLE-SOURCING VERIFIED. A mint is also dangerous when a second declaration desynchronises. A sweep of the tree for version declarations finds exactly ONE: the `pyproject.toml` line itself. There is no `__version__` constant, no duplicated literal in the package, and no second manifest to drift. Parsing the manifest with the stdlib TOML reader confirms it resolves to `0.4.5` for the expected distribution name.

THE DELETION IS THE CORRECT CONSUMPTION OF A CREDENTIAL-LIKE ARTIFACT. The removed file is precisely the rc-1 verdict I authored, deleted in its own isolated commit (one file, 74 deletions, no other path). Because the covering-verdict routine treats such a record as authorization keyed on a PR head sha or its first parent, an un-consumed verdict is a standing approval credential; deleting it on consumption is the law and the safe posture. Verified at the range head: a full tree listing for any path under a verdicts directory returns ZERO survivors. The standing-authorization surface remains at 0, holding the CWE-613 remediation I recorded closed in the rc-1 verdict.

SECRETS AND PRIVATE NAMES OVER ADDED LINES -- CLEAN. Scanning only the added lines for operator-home path prefixes, credential keywords, PEM key headers, private-IP literals, personal e-mail domains, cloud access-key IDs, platform token shapes, the operator's name, and every sibling repo slug on the denylist returns ZERO hits. I specifically confirmed that the packaging manifest's author contact line is untouched CONTEXT, not an added line: the manifest diff consists of exactly one removed and one added line, both the version. Nothing in this range introduces a new identifier of any kind.

BECAUSE THIS CYCLE ENDS IN A PUBLICATION, I REVIEWED THE PUBLISH PATH ITSELF, NOT JUST THE DIFF. A release review that only reads the diff misses the question that actually matters: how does the artifact get signed into the world, and what credential does that take. The release workflow's posture is strong on every axis I checked. There is no long-lived publishing credential at all -- publication uses OIDC trusted publishing (`id-token: write`), so there is no API token to store, rotate, leak or exfiltrate, which eliminates the entire standing-credential class rather than managing it and matches the law that credential material lives in exactly one operator-managed place. The publish action is pinned to a full commit sha rather than a floating tag, so a compromised or retagged upstream action cannot silently change what runs at publish time (unpinned-action risk, CWE-1357, mitigated). Publication is gated behind an explicit manual approval job and a protected deployment environment, so the release cannot fire automatically off a merge. A scan of the workflow tree for credential-shaped literals, excluding legitimate secret and variable references, returns nothing. A post-publish install-and-smoke-run step verifies the artifact that actually landed. This range modifies none of that wiring -- no workflow file is touched -- so the posture described is the one that will execute.

SPECS DOCTOR SPOT-CHECK. A version mint can interact with the rule pinning the manifest version to the active release id, so I checked rather than assumed: the doctor reports 0 errors. The pin rule does not fire because the release in question is archived rather than active. The single warning is a pre-existing canonical-source drift on a scoped governance file that this range does not touch, where auto-overwrite is deliberately disabled to protect operator customisation; it is recorded below as record-only and is not ship-blocking.

SUITE NOT RE-RUN, PER INSTRUCTION. Preflight is reported green at this head (2879 passed, mypy strict, 7/7 import contracts). I did not re-execute it. That is a reasonable basis here precisely BECAUSE the range contains zero code and zero test changes -- there is no mechanism by which this diff could alter a test outcome.

RC-1 EVIDENCE CARRIED FORWARD (the content being shipped). The substantive security review of everything in this release was performed across the rc-1 cycle and is unchanged: the scan over every added line produced only false positives in three classes (an LLM budget/mode use of the word 'token', the NAME of the scan engine being relocated, and the regex SOURCE of the credential detector itself), with all high-risk subsets returning zero; the denylist push gate exited 0 on the reviewed range; public-asset privacy reported ok with an independent grep of every touched public asset yielding only two provable false positives; zero dependency changes and therefore zero new CVE surface; zero skip/xfail/quarantine markers added, with both deleted test files paired to their feature deletions and PINNED by assertions that they stay deleted; and the relocation of the secret-scan engine was proved lossless structurally -- all three data structures AST-identical, 7 rules before and 7 after in the same order, the scanner function body byte-identical after name normalisation, both call sites preserved and the consumer identity confirmed live and pinned by a committed test. The purge of six consumed verdict handoffs took the standing-authorization surface from 6 to 0, remediating the CWE-613 LOW I raised earlier.

BUG-SURFACE DELTA (operator standing order): UNCHANGED for executable surface, slightly REDUCED overall -- evidence in metrics.bug_surface_evidence.

CHAIN OF CUSTODY. This verdict names dc66121c. The rc-2 PR head will be the commit carrying these verdict files, whose first parent is dc66121c, so the two-hop covering rule (PR head, or head's first parent) resolves it. It must be deleted once that PR merges.

findings.message: Positive, and the decisive check for this range: the mint to 0.4.5 was verified against the live package index. No 0.5.x was ever published, 0.4.5 is unclaimed, and 0.4.5 is a strict increment over the true latest -- so there is no version shadowing and no silent downgrade.
findings.detail_md:
Reported as a supply-chain integrity **confirmation**, because the change has the shape of a dangerous one and therefore deserved measurement rather than trust.

**The risk considered.** The manifest moves from a higher internal spec-release id to `0.4.5`. Had any `0.5.x` ever been published, shipping `0.4.5` afterwards would place the NEWER code behind a LOWER version while resolvers continued to serve the older, higher-numbered artifact as latest -- a silent downgrade-shadowing of the whole release, and the sort of defect that is invisible in a diff.

**What the live index actually says.**

| Question | Measured answer |
|---|---|
| Published versions | `0.1.0, 0.1.1, 0.1.2, 0.1.4, 0.1.5, 0.1.6, 0.2.0, 0.2.1, 0.2.2, 0.2.3, 0.3.0, 0.4.0, 0.4.1, 0.4.2, 0.4.4` |
| Index `info.version` (latest) | `0.4.4` |
| Any `0.5.x` published? | **NONE** |
| Is `0.4.5` already taken? | **No** |

**Conclusion.** `0.4.5` is contiguous with the true latest `0.4.4`, collides with nothing (a re-upload would be refused by the index in any case), shadows nothing, and will correctly resolve as the new highest version. The CHANGELOG's amended sentence -- that the earlier internal id was staged but its publication was retained and never approved at the release gate -- is **confirmed true by the index**. Removing that false provenance claim from shipped documentation is itself an integrity improvement.

**Single-sourcing checked too.** A sweep for version declarations across the tree finds exactly one (the manifest line); there is no second constant or manifest that could drift out of agreement.
findings.fix_recommendation: No action. Recorded as the measured basis for authorizing publication at this number.

findings.message: Positive: the publish path uses OIDC trusted publishing with no long-lived credential, a sha-pinned publish action, a manual approval gate and a protected environment. This range modifies none of that wiring.
findings.detail_md:
Reviewed because this cycle ends with an artifact reaching the public index, so the credential path matters as much as the diff.

| Control | Observed |
|---|---|
| Publishing credential | OIDC trusted publishing (`id-token: write`) -- **no API token exists to leak or rotate** |
| Publish action integrity | pinned to a full commit sha, not a floating tag (unpinned-action risk, CWE-1357, mitigated) |
| Human gate | explicit manual approval job plus a protected deployment environment before publication |
| Hardcoded credentials | none -- a scan for credential-shaped literals, excluding legitimate secret/variable references, returns nothing |
| Post-publish verification | installs from the index and runs a smoke check on what actually landed |

Eliminating the long-lived token class outright is stronger than managing it, and it matches the law that credential material lives in exactly one operator-managed place and is never persisted into a repo, image, cache or report. **No workflow file is touched by this range**, so the posture described here is the one that will execute.

findings.message: The consumed rc-1 verdict is deleted in its own isolated commit and zero verdict survivors remain, holding the CWE-613 standing-authorization surface at 0.
findings.detail_md:
CWE-613 (insufficient credential expiration) -- **discipline holding**.

A verdict record is authorization: the covering-verdict routine qualifies a candidate on the PR head sha **or its first parent**, so any un-consumed verdict left on disk is a standing approval credential with no expiry. The range's deletion commit removes precisely the rc-1 verdict I authored -- one file, 74 deletions, no other path -- which is the correct consumption shape (consumed once by the merge, deleted after) and the correct commit isolation.

Verified at the range head rather than assumed: a full tree listing for any path under a verdicts directory returns **zero** entries. The surface remains at 0, holding the remediation I recorded closed in the rc-1 verdict. The two verdicts written for this ship cycle are themselves subject to the same rule and must be deleted once their PRs merge.
findings.fix_recommendation: After each merge, delete the consumed verdict. Both verdicts issued for this ship cycle (the rc-2 one and the ship one) must not survive their merges.
